theme: The anointing; the Entry; the grain of wheat must die
readingInstruction: Read John 12:1-50. Mary anoints Jesus, the crowds welcome him into Jerusalem, Greeks seek him, and he speaks of the grain of wheat that must die. The first half of John’s Gospel ends here. Read verses 23 to 33 slowly.
settingTheScene: Six days before Passover, Jesus returns to Bethany for a supper in his honor. Lazarus is at the table. Large crowds come to see both Jesus and Lazarus, and many are believing. Meanwhile the chief priests plot to kill Lazarus as well. Jesus enters Jerusalem to the shouts of the crowd. Then the “hour” that has been mentioned throughout the Gospel finally arrives.
observation: “Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume” (12:3).
“Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!” (12:13).
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (12:24).
“Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life” (12:25).
“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (12:32).
“They loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God” (12:43).
“I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness” (12:46).
“For I did not come to judge the world but to save the world” (12:47).
interpretation:
At the supper, Mary takes a pound of costly perfume, pours it on Jesus’ feet, and wipes them with her hair. The house fills with the fragrance. Judas objects, saying it should have been sold and given to the poor, though John says he was a thief. Jesus defends her: “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.” She gives extravagantly, and Jesus accepts it as worship.

The next day, a large crowd takes palm branches and goes out to meet him, shouting “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!” Jesus sits on a young donkey, as Zechariah foretold. The Pharisees say, “Look, the world has gone after him.”

Some Greeks, Gentiles who had come to worship at the feast, ask to see Jesus. When Philip and Andrew tell him, Jesus says, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” The hour he has been waiting for is here, and it is tied to the coming of the nations. Then he says, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” His death will not end his work but multiply it. And the principle applies to his followers: “Whoever loves his life loses it.”

Jesus is troubled: “Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? But for this purpose I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” A voice from heaven answers. Then he says, “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” John explains that he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die. The cross is the throne, and from it he draws people of every nation.

John closes the first half of the Gospel with a sad note. Despite so many signs, they did not believe, and John quotes Isaiah on hardness of heart. Some leaders believed but would not confess, “for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.” Jesus cries out once more: he has come as light, to save and not to judge.
connection: Zechariah 9:9 is the donkey. Psalm 118:25-26 is the hosanna. Isaiah 53:1 and 6:10 are quoted at the end. Numbers 21:8-9 is the lifted bronze serpent. Genesis 12:3 promised the blessing to all nations. Galatians 2:20 says we have been crucified with Christ. Philippians 3:7-8 counts everything as loss for the sake of Christ. Mark 14:3-9 and Matthew 26:6-13 tell the story of the anointing.
application:
Ask what extravagant act of love you might offer Jesus, in time or money or service.

Consider what it means for you to “die” like the grain of wheat: what are you holding that needs to fall into the earth?

Pray for the nations: that the Greeks of our day would see Jesus.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you pour out your best on Jesus, as Mary did.
Ask him to teach you what it means to die like the grain of wheat.
Tell him what you want to lay down.
